claims.text: Cr39Co18Fe18Ni18Al7 initially forms a homogeneous high-temperature BCC phase.
Phase destabilization in Cr39Co18Fe18Ni18Al7 is driven by differential diffusion rates among its constituent elements during cooling.
Al diffuses faster than the other relevant constituent elements under the proposed cooling conditions.
Faster-diffusing elements, particularly Al, segregate locally during cooling.
Local enrichment of faster-diffusing elements creates nanoscale chemical inhomogeneities.
The resulting local composition fluctuations reduce the thermodynamic barrier to phase separation.
Chemically enriched nanoscale regions act as nucleation sites for ordered or intermetallic secondary phases.
Moderate-to-slow cooling and intermediate-temperature thermal holding provide sufficient atomic mobility for segregation and secondary-phase formation.
Slow cooling followed by an isothermal hold near 600°C should produce detectable secondary phases.
The secondary phases produced by slow cooling and holding should be observable as ordered intermetallic precipitates by diffraction and microscopy.
Ultra-fast quenching suppresses diffusion sufficiently to inhibit elemental segregation.
Rapid quenching should preserve a predominantly homogeneous high-temperature BCC structure.
Additional alloying elements or processing variables may alter diffusion kinetics and segregation behavior enough to make the proposed mechanism inapplicable.
Cooling-rate-dependent phase evolution can be tested by comparing rapidly quenched samples with samples that are slowly cooled and held near 600°C.
XRD, TEM, EDS mapping, and DSC can be used to compare phase constitution, precipitates, elemental segregation, and thermal transitions between treatments.
Absence of secondary phases and local segregation in the slow-cooled and held samples relative to the quenched baseline would falsify the proposed mechanism.
Phase evolution that is independent of cooling rate would falsify the claim that differential diffusion drives the phase evolution.
